units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Logarithms, Standard Form and Logarithm Tables
objectives: Express large and small numbers in standard form and interpret powers of ten.
Use logarithm and antilogarithm tables to evaluate products, quotients, roots and powers.
units.body:
LOGARITHMS AND STANDARD FORM

Standard form expresses a number as A x 10^n, where 1 <= A < 10 and n is an integer. Large numbers have positive powers of ten; numbers between zero and one use negative powers. Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit remains to its left and count the places moved to determine the exponent.

For positive numbers, log(ab)=log(a)+log(b), log(a/b)=log(a)-log(b), log(a^n)=n log(a), and log(root_n(a))=log(a)/n. A common logarithm has base 10. The integer part is the characteristic and the decimal part is the mantissa. For numbers less than one, use bar notation for a negative characteristic while retaining a positive mantissa. Antilog tables reverse the logarithm process.

When using tables, retain sufficient figures during intermediate steps and round only the final answer to the requested significant figures. Check that the magnitude of the answer is reasonable before accepting it.

units.title: Approximations, Significant Figures and Percentage Error
objectives: Round values to a stated number of significant figures and decimal places.
Calculate absolute, relative and percentage error and determine upper/lower bounds.
units.body:
APPROXIMATION AND PERCENTAGE ERROR

An approximation replaces an exact value with a nearby value at a stated degree of accuracy. Significant figures begin at the first non-zero digit; leading zeros are not significant. When rounding, inspect the digit immediately after the last retained digit. If it is 5 or greater, increase the last retained digit by one; otherwise leave it unchanged.

The absolute error is the magnitude of the difference between a measured/approximated value and the true value. Percentage error = (absolute error / true value) x 100%. If a measurement is rounded to the nearest unit, its maximum absolute error is half a unit. The smallest and largest possible values lie half a unit below and above the stated rounded value.

For derived quantities such as perimeter or area, calculate bounds using the smallest and largest possible measurements. Keep the distinction between percentage error, absolute error and percentage accuracy clear.

units.title: Sequences and Arithmetic Progression
objectives: Identify a sequence and determine its pattern and nth term.
Calculate terms, common difference and sums of arithmetic progressions.
units.body:
SEQUENCES AND ARITHMETIC PROGRESSION

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers formed according to a rule. An arithmetic progression (A.P.) is a sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms is constant. The first term is a, common difference is d, and the nth term is Tn=a+(n-1)d. A positive d gives an increasing A.P.; a negative d gives a decreasing A.P.

The sum of the first n terms is Sn=n/2[2a+(n-1)d], or Sn=n/2(a+l), where l is the last term. To solve a word problem, identify the first term, common difference and number of terms, then choose the nth-term or sum formula. A sequence may also be described by a rule such as Tn=3n-5; substitute n to obtain a specified term.

Check the pattern by calculating successive differences. Do not assume a sequence is arithmetic unless the difference is constant.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Geometric Progression and Geometric Series
objectives: Identify a geometric progression and calculate its common ratio and nth term.
Find finite sums and sums to infinity where they exist.
units.body:
GEOMETRIC PROGRESSION

A geometric progression (G.P.) is a sequence in which the ratio between consecutive terms is constant. The first term is a and the common ratio is r. The nth term is Tn=ar^(n-1). To find r, divide a term by the preceding term, checking that the ratio is consistent throughout the sequence.

The sum of the first n terms is Sn=a(1-r^n)/(1-r) when r is not 1, or a(r^n-1)/(r-1). If the absolute value of r is less than one, the infinite series converges and S-infinity=a/(1-r). If the absolute value of r is at least one, the ordinary infinite sum does not converge.

For word problems, identify whether the question asks for one term, a finite sum, or a sum to infinity. Use signed values for negative common ratios and check the number of terms carefully.

units.title: Quadratic Equations from Sum and Product of Roots
objectives: Construct a quadratic equation when the sum and product of roots are given.

units.body:
QUADRATIC EQUATIONS AND ROOT RELATIONSHIPS

A quadratic equation has the form ax^2+bx+c=0, where a is not zero. If its roots are alpha and beta, then alpha+beta=-b/a and alpha beta=c/a. Conversely, if the sum of roots is S and product is P, a monic quadratic equation is x^2-Sx+P=0. Multiplying through by a non-zero constant gives an equivalent equation.

Expressions involving roots can be simplified using the sum and product. For example, alpha^2+beta^2=(alpha+beta)^2-2alpha beta. The reciprocal sum 1/alpha+1/beta equals (alpha+beta)/(alpha beta), provided neither root is zero. Word problems can be translated into quadratic equations by defining an unknown, expressing the other quantity in terms of it, and using the given sum, difference, area or product.

Check candidate roots by substitution and interpret whether negative values are meaningful in the context of the problem.

objectives: Solve pairs of linear equations by elimination and substitution.

units.body:
SIMULTANEOUS LINEAR EQUATIONS

A pair of simultaneous linear equations has a common solution that satisfies both equations. The elimination method adds or subtracts suitably multiplied equations to remove one unknown. The substitution method makes one unknown the subject in one equation and substitutes it into the other. After finding one variable, substitute back to obtain the second and check both values in the original equations.

A pair of straight lines may intersect at one point, be parallel with no solution, or coincide with infinitely many solutions. The point of intersection is the ordered pair satisfying both line equations. Word problems involving ages, costs or quantities can be represented by defining two unknowns and forming two independent equations.

Use exact fractions where the solution is not an integer; do not round intermediate values unnecessarily.

units.body:
SIMULTANEOUS LINEAR AND QUADRATIC EQUATIONS

A simultaneous system containing one linear and one quadratic equation may have two, one or no real points of intersection. Make one variable the subject of the linear equation and substitute into the quadratic equation. Simplify to a single quadratic, solve by factorisation or the quadratic formula, then substitute each root back to obtain the corresponding value of the other variable.

A difference of two squares can simplify some systems. For example, x^2-y^2=(x-y)(x+y). If one equation is y=x^2 and the other is y=x+6, equate the right-hand sides to obtain a quadratic in x. The ordered pairs are the intersection points of the line and curve.

Check every ordered pair in both original equations; a sign error during factorisation can remove a valid solution or introduce an invalid one.

objectives: Calculate gradient and equation of a straight line from coordinates or a point and gradient.

units.body:
STRAIGHT-LINE GRAPHS AND GRADIENT

The gradient of a straight line measures its steepness and is calculated as change in y divided by change in x: m=(y2-y1)/(x2-x1). A line rising from left to right has positive gradient; one falling from left to right has negative gradient; a horizontal line has zero gradient. The equation can be written y=mx+c, where c is the y-intercept, or y-y1=m(x-x1) when a point and gradient are known.

A curve has a changing gradient. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent at that point and calculate the gradient of the tangent using two well-separated points on it. The accuracy depends on the scale and quality of the graph and tangent. The source includes plotting straight lines and curves, completing tables of values and estimating gradients.

For a line equation, rearrange into y=mx+c to read off the gradient and intercept. For graph questions, label axes, choose a clear scale and show the points used in the gradient calculation.

FIRST-TERM REVISION

The First-Term scheme lists Week 10 as Revision. This unit is therefore a cumulative review of the source-backed work: logarithms and standard form; approximation and percentage error; arithmetic and geometric progressions; quadratic equations from root relationships; simultaneous linear equations; simultaneous linear/quadratic systems; and straight-line graphs and gradients.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Revision and Straight-Line Graphs: Gradients and Tangents
objectives: Recall coordinate points, intercepts and simultaneous solution of two straight-line equations.
Calculate gradients and equations of straight lines, and interpret the gradient of a curve using a tangent.
units.body:
COORDINATE GEOMETRY AND STRAIGHT LINES

A point in the Cartesian plane is written (x,y): the x-coordinate is the abscissa and the y-coordinate is the ordinate. For a line y=mx+c, m is the constant gradient and c is the y-intercept. To find an x-intercept set y=0; to find a y-intercept set x=0. The intersection of two straight lines is found by solving their equations simultaneously.

For points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2), the gradient is m=(y2-y1)/(x2-x1), provided x2 is not x1. A line through (x1,y1) with gradient m has equation y-y1=m(x-x1). The gradient is also tan(theta), where theta is the angle of inclination measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.

The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent at that point. Draw the tangent carefully and choose two well-separated points on the tangent to estimate its gradient. At a smooth turning point the tangent is horizontal and the gradient is zero. Preserve scale and coordinate labels when drawing or reading a graph.

units.title: Inequalities in Two Variables and Combined Ranges
objectives: Represent a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane on the coordinate plane.
Solve simultaneous inequalities and express a combined range using interval notation.
units.body:
A linear inequality in two variables has a form such as ax+by<=c. Its boundary is the straight line ax+by=c. Draw the boundary using its intercepts or another pair of points. Use a solid line when equality is included (<= or >=) and a dashed line when it is excluded (< or >). Test a point not on the line, commonly (0,0), to decide which half-plane satisfies the inequality.

A combined inequality describes values that satisfy more than one condition at the same time. Solve each inequality separately, then take the overlap. For example, 2x+6>2 gives x>-2, while x-4<1 gives x<5; together they give -2<x<5. On a number line the common interval is between -2 and 5, with both endpoints open.

The source includes a worked half-plane example and asks learners to shade the solution region. The extracted mathematical signs in some lines are incomplete; use the original printed page when reconciling exact inequalities and graphs.

units.title: Applications of Inequalities in Two Variables
objectives: Translate practical restrictions into linear inequalities.
Use a graph and feasible region to determine possible and extreme values.
units.body:
Practical problems can be modelled with inequalities. Define each variable clearly, translate every restriction into a mathematical statement, and include non-negativity when the variables represent counts or quantities. A maximum capacity becomes <=; a minimum requirement becomes >=; a strict requirement such as “more than half” becomes >.

For a class with g girls and b boys and a maximum of 40 pupils, b+g<=40. If more than half the class are boys, then b>(b+g)/2, which simplifies to b>g. If there are at least 14 girls, g>=14. The feasible region is the intersection of these half-planes. Because pupils are counted, final solutions must be whole numbers.

The source also models a business employing men and women subject to a total staffing limit, minimum numbers for each role, and asks learners to identify maxima and minima from the graph. Check that the selected point satisfies every inequality, not just one boundary.

units.title: Algebraic Fractions: Simplification
objectives: Factorise numerators and denominators before cancelling common factors.
State the excluded values that make an original denominator zero.
units.body:
An algebraic fraction is simplified by factorising its numerator and denominator completely and cancelling common factors. Useful identities include x^2-y^2=(x-y)(x+y), (x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2 and (x-y)^2=x^2-2xy+y^2. Cancellation is permitted only for common factors, not for individual terms joined by addition or subtraction.

For example, (x^2-9)/(x^2+5x+6) becomes ((x-3)(x+3))/((x+2)(x+3)) and simplifies to (x-3)/(x+2). The original denominator is zero at x=-2 and x=-3, so both values remain excluded even though the factor (x+3) has cancelled.

units.title: Operations in Algebraic Fractions
objectives: Add and subtract algebraic fractions using a common denominator.
Multiply and divide algebraic fractions by factorising and cancelling valid common factors.
units.body:
To add or subtract algebraic fractions, first find a common denominator. Rewrite each fraction with that denominator, combine the numerators, then factorise and simplify. Do not add denominators. For multiplication, multiply numerators together and denominators together, then cancel common factors. For division, invert the second fraction and multiply; the divisor must not be zero.

For example, 1/(x-1)+1/(x+1) has common denominator (x-1)(x+1)=x^2-1. The numerator is (x+1)+(x-1)=2x, so the result is 2x/(x^2-1), where x is not 1 or -1. Check restrictions from the original expressions and from any divisor.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Logic: Propositions, Connectives and Valid Arguments
objectives: Distinguish simple and compound propositions and construct truth tables for logical connectives.
Recognise conditional, converse, inverse, contrapositive, tautology, contradiction and valid argument.
units.body:
A proposition is a statement that is either true (T) or false (F), but not both. A simple proposition contains no logical connective; a compound proposition combines propositions. The main connectives are conjunction (p and q), disjunction (p or q), conditional (if p then q), biconditional (p if and only if q) and negation (not p).

Conjunction is true only when both statements are true. Disjunction is false only when both are false. The conditional p->q is false only when p is true and q is false. The biconditional is true when p and q have the same truth value. A tautology is always true; a contradiction is always false. The converse of p->q is q->p; the inverse is not-p -> not-q; the contrapositive is not-q -> not-p. A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent.

An argument has premises and a conclusion. It is valid when true premises cannot lead to a false conclusion. Distinguish inductive reasoning, which generalises from observations, from deductive reasoning, which derives a conclusion from stated premises. The source includes truth tables and a comparison between algebra of sets and algebra of propositions.

objectives: Apply the theorem that an angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.

For a fixed arc of a circle, the angle subtended at the centre is twice the angle subtended at any point on the remaining circumference. Therefore, if the central angle is 120 degrees, the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc is 60 degrees. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle because the angle at the centre is 180 degrees and the circumference angle is half of it.

Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal when they stand on the same chord or arc. units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Cyclic Quadrilaterals
objectives: Identify a cyclic quadrilateral and use its opposite-angle property.

units.body:
A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on one circle. Its opposite interior angles are supplementary: each opposite pair adds to 180 degrees. If one angle is 108 degrees, the opposite angle is 72 degrees. The property follows because each angle at the circumference is related to the arc opposite it, and the arcs around the circle total 360 degrees.

When solving a diagram, first confirm that all four vertices lie on the circumference. Label the opposite pair, write their sum as 180 degrees, and solve the resulting equation. Do not apply the property to an arbitrary quadrilateral that is not cyclic. The source Week 11 body proves the supplementary-angle theorem and assigns a proof involving a tangent and a chord; the exact assignment wording and diagrams still need page-level reconciliation.

units.title: Tangents to Circles and Alternate-Segment Angles
objectives: Prove and apply the theorem that tangents from an external point are equal.
Use the radius-tangent right angle and the alternate-segment theorem to calculate unknown angles.
units.body:
A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point. Triangles OAT and OBT are congruent by RHS: OA and OB are radii, OT is common, and each radius meets its tangent at 90 degrees. The line OT bisects the angle between the tangents.

The alternate-segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle in the opposite segment subtended by that chord. Identify the chord and tangent carefully before applying the theorem. objectives: Use the sine rule to find unknown sides or angles in acute and obtuse triangles.

units.body:

The cosine rule is c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab cos C, with analogous forms for a and b. Use it when two sides and their included angle are known, or rearrange it to find an angle from three sides. After calculating an angle, check that the sum of the triangle's angles is 180 degrees and that the result is consistent with the side lengths.

objectives: Measure bearings clockwise from north and express them as three-figure angles.

Use sine, cosine or tangent according to the known and required sides of the right triangle.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Grouped Data: Class Boundaries, Class Marks and Histograms
objectives: Convert stated class limits to continuous class boundaries and calculate class marks.
Construct and interpret cumulative frequencies and histograms for grouped data.
units.body:
For grouped data, a class interval has a lower and upper limit. If measurements are recorded to the nearest whole unit, subtract 0.5 from each lower limit and add 0.5 to each upper limit to obtain continuous class boundaries. The class mark (midpoint) is (lower boundary+upper boundary)/2. The class width is the difference between the boundaries.

A cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies up to a class. A histogram represents grouped continuous data with adjacent rectangles. When class widths are unequal, use frequency density (frequency divided by class width) for the bar height; with equal widths, frequency can be used directly. Label the horizontal axis with class boundaries and the vertical axis with frequency or frequency density as appropriate.

units.title: Mean, Median and Mode of Grouped Data
objectives: Calculate the mean of grouped data using class marks and frequencies.
Estimate the median and mode from grouped frequency distributions.
units.body:
For grouped data, calculate each class mark x as the midpoint of its class boundaries. Multiply each class mark by its frequency f, then find the mean using sum(fx)/sum(f). Keep a table of class intervals, class marks, frequencies and fx so the calculation can be checked.

The median class contains the N/2-th observation, where N is the total frequency. For continuous grouped data, an estimated median is L+[(N/2-cf)/f]h, where L is the lower boundary of the median class, cf is the cumulative frequency before it, f is the median-class frequency and h is the class width. An estimated mode for a grouped distribution is L+[(f1-f0)/(2f1-f0-f2)]h, where f1 is the modal-class frequency and f0 and f2 are the preceding and following frequencies.

units.title: Probability: Events, Outcomes and Sample Spaces
objectives: Define a random experiment, event, outcome and sample space.
Calculate theoretical and experimental probabilities for simple events.
units.body:
A random experiment is a process whose result is not known in advance. A trial is one performance of the experiment. An outcome is a possible result, an event is a specified set of outcomes, and the sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes. The number of outcomes is written n(S); the number belonging to event E is n(E).

For equally likely outcomes, P(E)=n(E)/n(S). Probability is between 0 and 1. An impossible event has probability 0 and a certain event has probability 1. For two tosses of a fair coin, S={HH,HT,TH,TT}; the event “exactly one head” contains HT and TH, so its probability is 2/4=1/2. Experimental probability is the observed frequency of an event divided by the number of trials; it may approach theoretical probability as the number of trials increases.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Probability Laws, Independent Events and Tree Diagrams
objectives: Apply addition and multiplication rules to mutually exclusive and independent events.
Use tree diagrams to solve probability problems with and without replacement.
units.body:
Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B). For any event A, the complement has probability P(not A)=1-P(A). Independent events do not affect one another; for independent A and B, P(A and B)=P(A)P(B). Do not use the independent-event multiplication rule for dependent selections without replacement.

A tree diagram shows each possible sequence of outcomes. Write the probability on each branch and multiply along a path to find the probability of that sequence. Add the probabilities of separate paths when any of them satisfy the required event. With replacement, the composition of the bag is restored before the second selection, so the branch probabilities remain the same. Without replacement, the total and colour counts change after the first draw.

The source treats mutually exclusive and independent events, addition and multiplication laws, and tree-diagram applications. Its weekend assignment includes two-dice sums and coloured-ball selections; all exact source item wording, options and mark allocations remain to be reconciled.
